paragraphs.dominant_move: management decision and common capacity objective
shared daylight, campsite, demand, and trip assumptions
analytic base case and its restrictive reference role
agent model mechanism and departure-time recommendation
itinerary model mechanism and fixed-schedule recommendation
probability model mechanism and cutoff recommendation
model-specific capacity values and common reported range
manager-facing choice among safety, autonomy, and crowding tradeoffs
rising rafting demand, overcrowding risk, and one-group-per-campsite constraint
maximum-groups question and three-model comparison plan

global_organization_chain: The abstract forecasts the river-capacity decision, common assumptions, three model families, model-specific recommendations, and common reported range.
The manager memo translates the mathematical alternatives into safety, autonomy, crowding, maintenance, throughput, and implementation tradeoffs.
The introduction and parameter table turn rising demand and one-group-per-campsite occupancy into a typed capacity problem.
Shared and model-specific assumptions define daylight, season, river length, campsite geometry, craft speeds, trip durations, demand, and desired stopping behavior.
The analytic base case rescales time, speed, and spacing to derive a restrictive launch bound and staggered departure reference.
The agent model advances independent boats minute by minute, searches for campsites, records failures, and sweeps departure time, slow-boat duration, launch rate, and campsite count.
The itinerary model prioritizes slow boats, greedily selects feasible campsites near daily goals, rejects infeasible demand, and separates a comfortable threshold from an overdriven upper envelope.
The probability model conditions a stop process, argues for a nightly fleet distribution, decomposes blocking events, and reads a one-percent cutoff from six parameterized plots.
The conclusion compares model mechanisms and maps manager beliefs about fixed schedules and autonomous behavior to a recommended operating rule.
The extension section opens nonuniform campsite, correlated weather, and seasonal-demand directions while preserving the need for target-river calibration.

The final warning pass reconciles date, unit, season, symbol, algorithm, caption, probability, cutoff, spacing, completion, validation, and provenance defects without replacing positive learning artifacts.

main_argument_chains.claim: A restrictive analytic reference can link travel window, identical speed, campsite spacing, and daily launches.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use it as a transparent reference case, not a validated optimum, and separate the step function from any continuous relaxation.

main_argument_chains.claim: An autonomous minute-step boat model can relate departure timing and slow-boat trip length to failures and utilization.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Operational use requires exact event ordering, simultaneous-arrival handling, seeds, repetitions, raw outputs, uncertainty, and season-end censoring.

main_argument_chains.claim: A greedy fixed-itinerary model can reject infeasible demand before issuing schedules and can distinguish a comfortable threshold from an upper envelope.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat approximately 1260 retained trips as the stated comfortable regime and roughly 1400 as an overdriven envelope only after speed generation, rollback, rejected demand, completion, and uncertainty are specified.

main_argument_chains.claim: A conditional stochastic stop model can turn nightly boat positions and campsite blocking geometry into a cutoff probability.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Do not reuse the 77-boat cutoff until conditioning, steady state, event completeness, mixed-speed arrival order, and printed spacing labels are re-derived and calibrated.

main_argument_chains.claim: The paper's three model families report a similar seasonal range and support different manager control philosophies.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Present the range as shared-assumption triangulation rather than independent validation, and keep launches, concurrency, retained schedules, completions, and customers distinct.

warnings.warning: The manager memo is dated February 13, 2012, while the paper title page is dated February 12, 2012.
Boats, boaters, customers, groups, trips, and people served are used as if they were interchangeable throughput units.
May 1 through October 31 contains 184 calendar days when both endpoints are included, not the stated 180 days.
The Grand Canyon coordinates omit explicit minute and second marks, making the printed coordinate notation ambiguous.
Perfectly even campsite spacing drives all three models but is not supported by target-river data.
The exponential stopping model supplies no rate parameter, scale, unit, or calibration from trip duration.
The paper differentiates n after defining daily capacity with a floor; the displayed derivatives apply only to an unstated continuous surrogate, not the step function itself.
The base-case description says newly launched boats fill sites 1 through k even though k is not defined in the parameter table or derivation.
The agent simulation does not specify random seed, repeat count, boat ordering within each minute, simultaneous campsite arrival resolution, or closed-season censoring.
Figure 2's caption says percent of boats failing, but its vertical axis and data show campsite utilization.
Figures 2 and 3 repeat essentially the same slow-boat minimum-night utilization curve without explaining the duplication.
Several figure captions print Delta where the plot title uses Delta X, weakening symbol consistency.
The agent failure curve and the claimed seasonal capacity are not connected by a reproducible table, seed, repeated-run interval, or exact interpolation rule.
The 1170 seasonal-trip claim does not state whether it counts launches or completed trips and does not reconcile end-of-season boats still on the river.
The itinerary target formula uses L without defining it and hard-codes i=1,...,6 although the algorithm later evaluates seven or more daily rafts.
The itinerary algorithm sorts by boat speed but its boat-generation step explicitly samples duration only, leaving speed generation implicit.
Removing a boat after a greedy placement failure does not specify whether prior placements are rolled back or the schedule is recomputed.
The prose cites Figure 11 as campsite utilization versus campsite count, but Figure 11 is failed rafts; Figure 12 is the utilization plot.
The paper calls Delta X at least seven an overdrive even though seven is also its stated carrying-capacity boundary; strict overdrive would begin above seven.
The claim that utilization approaches 100 percent is based on a plotted plateau around 94 to 95 percent and no exact data table.
Figure 14 places the Delta X=7 failed-boat mean speed closer to 8 mph than the prose value of approximately 7.5 mph.
The probability model combines unconditional independent exponential increments with a fixed total stop count without explicitly conditioning the Poisson process.
The nightly uniform fleet argument requires steady state, equal stage representation, common support, independence, and ignored start/end transients that are not fully stated.
The text says K is Binomial(N-1,2), using 2 where a binomial success probability such as w is required.
The printed P(B) factor C(2,1)w(1-w) is not the conditional split probability of one boat in w and one in the adjacent D interval after conditioning on two boats in w+D.
The two displayed equal-speed events are not a complete general cutoff calculation unless delta's campsite interval, direction, occupancy, and all blocking configurations are fixed.
The mixed-speed formulas replace geometric threatening regions with p_f-scaled interval lengths without deriving the needed joint position, type, speed, and arrival-order probabilities.
The probability plots are described as travel of 14 miles without consistently distinguishing exactly 14, at least 14, and more than 14 miles.
A 1.25-mile spacing is not one hundredth of a 225-mile river and would imply roughly 180 intervals, not the printed 99 campsites.
The 77/12 times 180 calculation counts launches under a 180-day approximation and does not require those trips to finish within the season.
Agreement among the three models is not independent validation because they share river length, even campsite spacing, controlled demand assumptions, season horizon, and throughput ambiguities.
No executable code, seed, simulation configuration, raw output table, uncertainty analysis, or frozen source archive is provided.
The reference gives Ithica, NY for Cornell University; the place name is Ithaca.
